posts.title: Cleanup Day: Portfolio Goes 3D, GitHub Gets a Real Home
posts.content:
Spent about 4 hours today turning my portfolio from a static page into something I'll actually 
be proud to send recruiters for years to come.

What I did:
- Added a 3D animated background and tilting project cards using Three.js
- Fixed the blog so posts are actually visible to visitors (not just stuck in my own browser)
- Deployed the whole thing live on GitHub Pages at m-m-s-b-s.github.io
- Cleaned up my GitHub profile to look more professional
- Hunted down a stubborn bug where my profile photo kept disappearing — turned out to be a 
  hidden script silently swapping it for a broken backup image on every page load
- Locked down the admin panel with a real password instead of the default one

Biggest lesson: shipping something publicly always surfaces problems you'd never catch testing 
locally. Every browser, every device showed me something different. Debugging that patiently, 
one layer at a time, taught me more about how the web actually works than any tutorial would.

Next up: fixing my project links so they point straight to my repos, and getting a real domain 
name.

posts.title: Two Sides of the Morning Commute on the Tobu Tojo Line
posts.content:
The morning rush hour on the Tobu Tojo Line is legendary for a reason. Boarding a packed train from Shiki to Ikebukuro on a standard Thursday morning offers a raw, unfiltered snapshot of Tokyo commuter life—one that often reveals stark contrasts in how people react under pressure.

The Clash of Cultures and Conscience
Boarding at Asakadai, the carriage was already a wall of bodies when an Arabic-speaking family squeezed on. Amidst the crush, a mother stood in the silver priority seating area trying to comfort a baby crying loudly. Given the overwhelming crowd, they quickly decided to cut their losses and planned to get off at the very next stop, Wakoshi.

Then came the typical commuter friction: a Japanese salaryman, desperate to make space or push his way further in, shoved hard against the passengers blocking the doorway. The force rippled backward. I locked eyes with him, alongside two Japanese women and another man trapped in the rear. Based on the family’s hurried Arabic conversation, the sudden shove had clearly hurt the mother and her two children.

Yet, the most jarring part wasn't the physical shove—it was the collective glare from surrounding commuters. Not directed at the aggressive push, but at the family for daring to speak aloud about their distress.

A Different Kind of Wake-Up Call
A few stops later at Wakoshi station, the narrative shifted entirely. Two Vietnamese travelers with oversized luggage attempted to board our packed car (Car 4-2). Wedged tightly on the threshold, they struggled against the human barrier trying to force their way in.

Instead of cold stares, a young Japanese man stepped in to help manage the chaos. Granted, his choice of words was blunt—he barked "Okiro!" (Wake up / Get moving!), which is far too informal for polite company—but his underlying action was helpful, guiding them through the tight squeeze.

By the time the train crawled into Narimasu, the claustrophobia won out, and I pushed my way off the carriage early.

The Takeaway
Japan's transit system runs with unmatched precision, but the human element inside the metal tubes is a complex ecosystem. In the span of a single commute, you can witness the cold intolerance of social pressure and the pragmatic, if rough-edged, kindness of a stranger. It is all part of the daily rhythm of life on the rails.

What unexpected moments have you witnessed during your morning rush hour? Let’s talk in the comments below.

posts.title: From Zero to Web Security: My Kali Linux Journey
posts.content:
A hands-on, beginner-friendly path through Kali Linux — from installing VirtualBox to running real SQL injection and XSS attacks on legal practice labs. Written so anyone can follow along without needing help from anyone else.

## Why I Started This

I'm a Digital Business and Innovation student, and before this I had never opened a terminal. I started this project over a summer break with one goal: learn enough Kali Linux and web security, from scratch, to actually understand how systems get broken into — and how to stop it.

I didn't know Linux, I didn't know networking, and my Python was shaky. What I did have was time, three full free days a week, and a willingness to type every single command myself instead of just watching tutorials. This post is the full path I took, in order, with every command and explanation included — so if you're starting from the same zero I was, you can follow it without needing anyone's help.

## Setting Up the Lab

Kali Linux is a Linux distribution that comes preloaded with security and penetration-testing tools. You don't install it on your real computer — you run it inside a **virtual machine**, a "computer inside your computer," so it's fully isolated and safe to experiment in.

**What you need:** a 64-bit computer, ideally 8GB+ RAM, about 30GB free disk space, and virtualization enabled in your BIOS (usually on by default on modern machines).

**Step 1 — Install VirtualBox.** Go to [virtualbox.org](https://virtualbox.org), click Download, pick the version for your operating system (Windows, Mac, Linux), run the installer, and click through the defaults.

**Step 2 — Download Kali's pre-built VM image.** Go to [kali.org](https://kali.org) → **Get Kali** → **Virtual Machines** → choose the **VirtualBox** image. This downloads as a large `.7z` compressed file — the pre-built image is far faster than installing from an ISO.

**Step 3 — Unzip it.** Install [7-Zip](https://7-zip.org) (free), then right-click the downloaded `.7z` file → **7-Zip** → **Extract Here**. This creates a folder containing a `.vbox` file.

**Step 4 — Import into VirtualBox.** Open VirtualBox, click **Add**, and select that `.vbox` file. Kali now appears in your VM list.

**Step 5 — Start it.** Select Kali, click **Start**, and wait for the login screen. Log in with:

- Username: `kali`
- Password: `kali`

If you land on a desktop with the Kali dragon logo, you're done — the whole lab is set up.

> **One rule before you touch anything else:** Kali's tools are completely legal to learn with. What's illegal is pointing them at systems you don't own and don't have explicit permission to test. Every example in this post runs either on your own machine, your own home network, or on practice sites that explicitly invite you to attack them.

## Linux Fundamentals

Open the terminal (the small black-screen icon near the top-left of the Kali desktop). Everything below is typed there.

**Finding your way around:**

```bash
whoami      # who am I logged in as
pwd         # which folder am I standing in
ls          # what's in this folder
ls -la      # show hidden files (dotfiles) and full details
cd foldername   # move into a folder
cd ..       # move back up one level
```

**Creating and handling files:**

```bash
mkdir learning              # make a new folder
touch notes.txt              # create an empty file
echo "some text" > notes.txt    # write text into a file (overwrites)
echo "more text" >> notes.txt   # append text to a file
cat notes.txt                 # read a file's contents
cp notes.txt backup.txt       # copy a file
mv backup.txt renamed.txt     # move or rename a file
rm note.txt                   # delete a file
find /home/kali -name "*.txt"  # search for files anywhere, wildcards included
wc notes.txt                  # count lines, words, characters in a file
```

**Permissions — the part that confuses most beginners.** Run `ls -la` and you'll see lines like:

```
-rw-rw-r-- 1 kali kali 65 Jul 15 11:59 notes.txt
```

The first character is `d` (a folder) or `-` (a file). The next nine characters are permissions in **three groups of three** — owner, group, everyone else:

- `r` = read, `w` = write, `x` = execute, `-` = not allowed

You change permissions with `chmod` using a number per group, where **r = 4, w = 2, x = 1** and you add them up:

| Number | Meaning | Common use |
|---|---|---|
| 700 | owner: rwx, nobody else: nothing | private files |
| 644 | owner: rw-, everyone: r-- | normal documents |
| 755 | owner: rwx, everyone: r-x | folders and programs |

Example: `chmod 644 notes.txt` makes a file normally readable and writable by you, read-only for everyone else.

**Two habits worth burning into memory:**

- **Tab** auto-completes file and folder names — type a few letters and press Tab instead of typing the whole name.
- **Ctrl+C** cancels whatever the terminal is doing. If you ever see a stuck prompt (like `dquote>`, meaning you left a quote mark unclosed), Ctrl+C gets you out.

## Installing Tools and Scanning Networks

Before installing anything on a fresh Linux system, refresh the list of available software:

```bash
sudo apt update              # refresh the software catalog (asks for your password: kali)
sudo apt install tree        # install a tool, e.g. tree (visualizes folders as a diagram)
```

`sudo` means "run this as administrator" — needed for system-level actions like installing software.

### Meet Nmap — the network scanner

Every device on a network has up to 65,535 "doors" called **ports**, and different services sit behind different ones. Nmap knocks on them and tells you which are **open** (something's listening), **closed** (nothing's there), or **filtered** (a firewall is silently blocking the probe).

```bash
nmap localhost                     # scan your own machine — always safe
nmap -T4 -F scanme.nmap.org        # -T4 = faster timing, -F = only top 100 ports (fast scan)
nmap -T4 -F -sV scanme.nmap.org    # -sV = detect the exact service VERSION behind each port
sudo nmap -O scanme.nmap.org       # -O = guess the operating system (unreliable through firewalls/VMs)
sudo nmap -sC -T4 -F scanme.nmap.org  # -sC = run Nmap's built-in scripts for extra automated recon
```

`scanme.nmap.org` is a server the Nmap project set up specifically so people can practice scanning it legally.

A real result looks like this:

```
PORT   STATE SERVICE VERSION
22/tcp open  ssh     OpenSSH 6.6.1p1 Ubuntu
80/tcp open  http    Apache httpd 2.4.7 ((Ubuntu))
```

Knowing the exact software version matters because specific versions have documented, searchable security weaknesses (catalogued as **CVEs** — Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures). This is the very first step of any real security assessment: figure out exactly what's running before anything else.

**Scanning your own network:**

```bash
ip a                        # find your own IP address and network range
nmap -T4 -F 10.0.2.0/24     # scan every device on that network (the /24 means the whole 10.0.2.x range)
nmap -T4 -F -oN myscan.txt scanme.nmap.org   # save scan results to a file instead of just the screen
```

> **Rule:** only ever scan machines you own, your own network, or sites that explicitly invite it (like scanme.nmap.org). Scanning anything else without permission is illegal, even if nothing is damaged — more on this at the end of this post.

## How the Web Works

Before any web security tool makes sense, you need to see what a website actually *is* underneath the pretty page your browser draws. `curl` fetches a page and prints the raw response — no rendering.

```bash
curl http://example.com        # fetch the raw HTML
curl -I http://example.com     # fetch only the HTTP headers
```

A page is just text in labeled boxes (`<tags>`): a `<head>` (styling and setup, invisible) and a `<body>` (the visible content). The headers are the invisible conversation that happens on every request:

```
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Server: cloudflare
Content-Type: text/html
Allow: GET, HEAD
```

`200 OK` means success (other key codes: `404` not found, `403` forbidden, `500` server error). `Server:` reveals the exact software running — valuable recon, the web equivalent of Nmap's version detection.

### GET vs POST

These are the two main ways a browser sends data to a server:

```bash
# GET — data rides in the URL itself, visible in the address bar, browser history, and server logs
curl "http://example.com/page?name=shakil&city=tokyo"

# POST — data rides in the request body, hidden from the URL
curl -X POST -d "name=shakil&city=tokyo" http://example.com/page
```

| | GET | POST |
|---|---|---|
| Data location | in the URL | in the body |
| Visible in URL/history? | Yes | No |
| Typical use | reading/searching | logins, forms, payments |

One important nuance: POST hiding data from the URL is **not the same as encryption**. The data can still be read in transit unless the connection uses **HTTPS**. That's why every login page you trust starts with `https://`, not `http://`.

## Burp Suite

Normally your browser talks straight to a website and you never see the conversation. **Burp Suite is a proxy** — it sits in the middle, catching every request before it leaves your machine, so you can read it, change it, or let it through.

![How Burp Suite sits between your browser and the website](images/burp-proxy-flow.svg)

```bash
burpsuite   # launches it (comes preinstalled on Kali)
```

On first launch: choose **Temporary project in memory** → **Next** → **Use Burp defaults** → **Start Burp**.

**To intercept a live request:**

1. Go to the **Proxy** tab → **Intercept** sub-tab → click **Intercept is off** so it reads **Intercept is on**.
2. Click **Open browser** — Burp's own browser opens, pre-wired to route through it.
3. Visit any site in that browser. The page will hang — Burp has frozen the request.
4. Switch back to Burp. You'll see the raw request waiting, something like:

```
GET / HTTP/1.1
Host: example.com
User-Agent: Mozilla/5.0 (X11; Linux x86_64) ...
```

That's the literal, invisible conversation your browser has with every website — including the User-Agent string that identifies your browser and OS to the server.

5. Click **Forward** to let the request through (the page loads normally), or **Drop** to kill it entirely.

That catch → inspect → forward loop is the core move behind almost all web application security testing: if you can read a request, you can also *change* it before sending it on.

## SQL Injection

Websites often build database questions out of what you type. A login might check: *"find the user WHERE username = '[what you typed]' AND password = '[what you typed]'."* **SQL injection** happens when a site drops your input into that question without checking it — so you can type something that *rewrites the question itself* instead of just answering it. It's #3 on the [OWASP Top 10](https://owasp.org/www-project-top-ten/) list of the most critical web risks.

I practiced this on [PortSwigger's Web Security Academy](https://portswigger.net/web-security) — free, legal labs built by the creators of Burp Suite, specifically designed to be attacked.

**Lab 1 — revealing hidden data.** A shop filters products by category, secretly adding `AND released = 1` to only show public items. In the URL:

```
/filter?category=Gifts
```

Changing it to:

```
/filter?category=Gifts'--+
```

adds a single quote (closing the category text early) and `--` (which means "ignore everything after this" in SQL) followed by a required space. The hidden `AND released = 1` filter gets commented out entirely — and every hidden item appears.

**Lab 2 — login bypass.** The same idea, applied to a login form. Typing this into the **username** field (leaving password blank):

```
administrator'--
```

logs you in as administrator with no real password — the injected `'--` erases the password check from the query entirely.

**Why it's dangerous:** pushed further, this same flaw can dump an entire database — every user's email, password hash, and personal data — not just reveal one hidden product. It's behind some of the largest data breaches in history.

**The fix (for anyone building their own site):** never drop user input straight into a database query. Use **parameterized queries**, which treat input as pure data that can never be interpreted as a command.

## Cross-Site Scripting (XSS)

SQL injection tricks the **database** into running your commands. **XSS tricks the browser** into running your code. If a site displays what you type back onto the page without cleaning it — a comment, a search term — and you type actual code instead of text, the browser doesn't just show it. It runs it.

On PortSwigger's **"Reflected XSS into HTML context with nothing encoded"** lab, there's a search box that echoes your search term back onto the page. Typing a normal word shows the reflection happening. Typing this instead:

```html
<script>alert(1)</script>
```

makes a popup box appear showing "1" — proof the browser executed your code rather than displaying it as text.

**Reflected vs. stored XSS:** reflected XSS (what's above) runs once, for whoever clicks a crafted link. **Stored XSS** is worse — the malicious script gets saved (e.g. in a comment) and runs automatically for *every single visitor* who views that page afterward.

**Why it's dangerous:** `alert(1)` is just a harmless proof-of-concept. Real injected code can silently steal a visitor's session cookie and send it to an attacker, effectively hijacking their logged-in session — without ever touching the server itself.

**The underlying pattern connects both vulnerabilities:** SQL injection and XSS are the same root mistake in two different places — **untrusted input treated as something executable instead of plain data.** The fix for XSS specifically is **encoding output** — making sure characters like `<` and `>` get displayed as harmless text instead of being interpreted as real HTML/code.

## Staying Legal

This is the single most important section of this post — more important than any command above it.

**The rule: only ever test systems you own, or systems you have explicit written permission to test.** Not "I was just curious." Not "I didn't change anything." Trying an attack technique against a real website or login page you don't have permission for is illegal in most countries — including, for example, under Japan's Unauthorized Computer Access Law. The *attempt itself* is the offense, whether or not it succeeds, and whether or not anything was damaged.

**How real attacks actually get noticed:**

- **Server and error logs** record every request, including your IP address and the exact payload you sent.
- **Web Application Firewalls (WAFs)** recognize textbook attack patterns like `'--` or `<script>` and can block and alert in real time.
- **Intrusion detection systems (IDS)** flag suspicious activity for a human to review.
- Your **IP address traces back to you** — there's no anonymity by default.

An injection attempt on a real site isn't a quiet whisper; it's a logged, often alarmed event with your address attached.

**If you want to test real, live systems legally:**

- **Bug bounty programs** (HackerOne, Bugcrowd) — companies that publicly invite testing and pay for valid findings.
- Ask an organization directly whether they have a responsible-disclosure policy.

Everything in this post was run either on my own machine, my own home network, or on platforms (`scanme.nmap.org`, PortSwigger's Web Security Academy) that explicitly exist for this purpose.

## Quick Reference: Every Command Used

| Command | What it does |
|---|---|
| `whoami` / `pwd` | who you are / where you are |
| `ls` / `ls -la` | list files / list all, including hidden, with details |
| `cd foldername` / `cd ..` | move into / out of a folder |
| `mkdir` / `touch` | make a folder / make an empty file |
| `echo "text" > file` / `>> file` | write to a file / append to a file |
| `cat file` | read a file |
| `cp` / `mv` / `rm` | copy / move-rename / delete |
| `find path -name "*.ext"` | search for files, with wildcards |
| `wc file` | count lines, words, characters |
| `chmod 700/644/755 file` | set who can read, write, run |
| `sudo` | run a command as administrator |
| `apt update` / `apt install X` | refresh software list / install a tool |
| `tree` | show folders as a visual diagram |
| `ip a` | show your own IP address and network |
| `nmap target` | scan a target's open ports |
| `nmap -T4 -F target` | faster scan, top 100 ports |
| `nmap -sV target` | detect exact service versions |
| `nmap -O target` | guess the operating system |
| `nmap -sC target` | run built-in recon scripts |
| `nmap -oN file.txt target` | save results to a file |
| `curl url` / `curl -I url` | fetch a page / fetch only its headers |
| `curl -X POST -d "k=v" url` | send data via POST |
| `burpsuite` | launch Burp Suite |

### What's Next

This is a foundation, not a finish line — nobody "masters" security, people just keep layering depth onto a base like this one. From here I'm continuing to solve labs on [PortSwigger's Web Security Academy](https://portswigger.net/web-security) independently, and working toward a recognized certification (CompTIA Security+, and eventually Japan's 基本情報技術者/FE exam) to turn this hands-on learning into something employers can verify.

If you're reading this as a fellow beginner: the biggest thing that made this stick wasn't any single command — it was typing every single one myself, slowly, over real weeks, instead of just watching someone else do it.
